p7_b0.ocr: In recent studies evaluating the ecological impacts of different pine species on larval survivorship, significant variations were observed between Pinus massoniana and Pinus elliottii. The data presented in the accompanying table highlights the percentage of larval survivorship associated with each species, along with metrics regarding previous-year and current-year needle production.

p7_b1.ocr: Notably, larval survivorship for P. massoniana was recorded at 46.00 ± 3.93%, showcasing a robust capacity for supporting larval populations. In contrast, P. elliottii displayed a markedly lower survivorship rate of 19.67 ± 3.98%.

p7_b3.ocr: These findings suggest that the ecological characteristics of each pine species can significantly influence the survivorship of larvae, potentially due to differences in needle quality or availability. Furthermore, the table delineates the relationship between needle age and larval survivorship, with current-year needles of P. massoniana appearing to enhance larval survival more effectively than previous-year needles.

p7_b4.ocr: This differentiation in survivorship rates underscores the importance of species selection in forest management practices, particularly in relation to biodiversity conservation and the sustainability of pest populations. Future research should further investigate the underlying mechanisms driving these differences to inform effective management strategies.
